analysis.one_liner: Bans flavored cigarettes and vapes, mandates graphic cigarette warnings, taxes vaping nicotine, and funds quit-smoking programs.
analysis.headline: The House passed the tobacco bill 213-195 on February 28, 2020, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would crack down on tobacco and e-cigarettes: graphic health warnings on cigarette packs, a ban on flavors including menthol cigarettes and flavored vapes, an end to online tobacco sales, higher FDA fees on manufacturers, an excise tax on vaping nicotine, and new rules for lab-made nicotine. It also funds smoking-cessation and prevention programs, especially in underserved communities, waives Medicare coinsurance for follow-up after colorectal cancer screening, and keeps high-deductible plans from charging a deductible for inhalers. The House passed it in February 2020; the Senate never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people: young people targeted by flavored vape marketing, adult smokers the bill would help quit, Black communities disproportionately marketed menthol cigarettes, and Medicare enrollees and people with chronic lung disease, who get out-of-pocket relief. Public health programs for prevention and cessation receive new funding.

how_it_helps.text: Requires color graphic warnings on cigarette packs depicting smoking's health consequences, and applies FDA tobacco advertising and sales rules to e-cigarettes like other tobacco products.

Bans characterizing flavors in tobacco products, including menthol cigarettes, and bars flavored e-cigarettes unless a maker proves the flavor helps smokers quit and does not attract youth; it also makes it unlawful to market vaping products to anyone under 21 and bars undisclosed paid promotion.
Generally prohibits online retail sales of tobacco products, so age checks happen face to face.

Funds prevention and cessation work through fiscal year 2025: $75 million a year for outreach and research, $75 million a year for demonstration grants in medically underserved communities, $45 million a year for a national youth awareness campaign, and $125 million a year for cessation treatment at health centers.

Starting in 2024, waives Medicare coinsurance when a colorectal cancer screening turns into a diagnostic procedure or polyp removal in the same visit, closing a surprise-billing gap; and lets high-deductible health plans cover inhalers and nebulizers before the deductible without losing their tax status.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco and vaping manufacturers, through higher FDA user fees ($812 million in fiscal 2021), the loss of flavored products including menthol, an excise tax on nicotine used in vaping, and a ban on online sales. Adult vapers and smokers who buy flavored products or shop online bear higher prices and lost convenience.

drawbacks.text: The flavor bans, including menthol cigarettes and flavored vapes, take away products some adult smokers use in place of cigarettes; whether e-cigarettes help people quit or hook new users was contested, and the bill requires a Government Accountability Office study on that relationship rather than resolving it.
The online-sales ban and the new excise tax on vaping nicotine make quitting aids and lower-risk alternatives more expensive and harder to get for adults in rural areas or with limited mobility.

The bill exempts premium cigars (hand-made, priced at $12 or more, rising with inflation) from premarket FDA review and from the online-sales ban, a carve-out for a small, well-connected corner of the tobacco industry that public health reviewers did not receive for cheaper products.

The menthol ban raised fairness concerns among some advocates for Black smokers, since menthol use is concentrated in Black communities; the bill responds by expressly barring criminal penalties or stops for individual possession and pairing the ban with cessation funding, but enforcement against sellers would still remove a product millions use daily.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is strong: tobacco remains the leading preventable cause of death, the bill targets the marketing channels (flavors, online sales, youth-oriented advertising) behind the youth vaping surge, and the Medicare and inhaler provisions directly cut out-of-pocket costs. The honest costs fall mostly on adult users of flavored products, and the premium-cigar exemption is a real hole carved for one industry. On balance the bill's benefits to ordinary people outweigh its costs, though the design choices on flavors would have forced some adults back toward riskier choices.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 213-195, but it went to the Senate Finance Committee on March 2, 2020, never got a vote or a hearing, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The House Energy and Commerce Committee reported the bill amended on a 28-24 vote in February 2020 after subcommittee work in late 2019.
The House passed the bill 213-195 on February 28, 2020: 208 of 232 Democrats voted yes while only 5 of 197 Republicans did, and the House's lone Independent voted no.
A Republican motion to recommit, which would have attached the 'Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection' title, failed 187-220, with 183 of 197 Republicans voting yes and 3 of 231 Democrats.
The Senate received the bill on March 2, 2020, and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where no further action was recorded before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill's text as passed the House carried a premium-cigar exemption from premarket review and from the online-sales ban, reflecting changes made during committee consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco and vaping companies came out ahead: no menthol ban, flavor restrictions, online-sales ban, or vaping nicotine tax ever took effect, and cigarette makers kept marketing menthol and flavored products through the pandemic and beyond.

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and moved it through subcommittee, a 28-24 committee vote, and House passage.

for.name: Public health groups including the American Lung Association and Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids
for.what_they_did: Backed the bill publicly as the strongest congressional response to youth vaping and menthol cigarettes.

against.name: Greg Walden
against.role: Ranking Member, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to attach the 'Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection' title; the motion failed 187-220, and he voted no on passage.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred never took it up; no markup, hearing, or vote is recorded before the Congress ended.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote in the ten months between House passage and the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split heavily by party, 208 of 232 Democrats yes versus 5 of 197 Republicans, and the motion to recommit was nearly all-Republican, 183 yea to 3 Democratic yea.

industries.note: The bill would require graphic warning labels, ban menthol and other characterizing flavors, and raise FDA user fees to $812 million in fiscal 2021. Menthol is a mainstay of cigarette sales, and the industry's interest in keeping it runs against the public-health goal.

The bill would ban flavored vapes absent a strict FDA finding, tax nicotine used in vaping at roughly the cigarette rate, restrict youth-appealing advertising, and cover synthetic nicotine under FDA authority. Vaping companies built their market on flavors and online sales, both of which the bill closes off.

industries.industry: Online tobacco retailers and vape shops
industries.note: The online-sales ban would shut remote sellers out of the market, but the face-to-face requirement shields brick-and-mortar shops from that competition even as flavor bans cut their product lines.

The bill exempts premium cigars from premarket FDA review and from the online-sales ban, a carve-out won during committee that spares the most expensive segment of the industry the scrutiny applied to all other tobacco products.

The bill makes it unlawful to market vaping products in a way that appeals to people under 21 and requires paid endorsements to be clearly disclosed, enforceable by the FTC and state attorneys general.
